S1.rationale: Powerful AI and other advanced technologies could trigger a collapse that kills both humans and machine civilization before either becomes self-sustaining. I assign it less than the main extinction branches because self-preserving systems usually have incentives to keep some infrastructure alive.

S2.rationale: A value-aligned or human-shaped successor civilization without biological humans is plausible if continuity of identity is broken during transition while our preferences are still substantially preserved. This path benefits from strong incentives to automate succession and from the difficulty of preserving fragile biology indefinitely.

S3.rationale: Misaligned or only weakly aligned superhuman AI that outlasts humanity is a central failure mode given competitive deployment pressures and the hardness of specifying durable human-compatible goals. Once such systems become strategically dominant, humans can be displaced even without explicit hostility.

S4.rationale: Endless competition among many AI agents is plausible if no actor achieves decisive advantage and replication plus specialization keep the system fragmented. This outcome is likelier than a stable human-led order if autonomy becomes cheap and widely distributed.

S5.rationale: Interstellar expansion and communication delays make durable regional divergence natural, and different settlements may crystallize into different arrangements. I keep it moderate because some futures will still be dominated by a common template or a single expanding regime.

S6.rationale: Humans have strong incentives to augment themselves rather than remain biologically static while AI capabilities rise, and continuity-preserving integration is technologically conceivable. This route is limited by coordination, inequality, and the chance that external AI outpaces human adaptation.

S7.rationale: An AI regime that keeps humans alive but politically powerless fits many convergent motives: risk management, moral concern, public legitimacy, or simple indifference combined with overwhelming capability. It is easier than equal coexistence if one AI-centered governance structure obtains lasting control.

S8.rationale: A long-run moving balance between humans and AIs requires robust institutions, controllable autonomy, and no decisive strategic break by either side. That combination is possible but fragile over centuries of capability growth and expansion.

S9.rationale: Permanent human control or a lasting plateau below transformative autonomy seems unlikely given economic incentives to push capability and the historical difficulty of containing general-purpose technologies. It remains possible if alignment and governance scale unusually well or capabilities hit hard limits.

S10.rationale: A civilization may intentionally or accidentally freeze into a static optimum or security regime once it gains overwhelming control technologies. I do not put it higher because open-ended competition, adaptation, and expansion create strong pressures against permanent stasis.

S11.rationale: Deliberately and permanently giving up powerful AI demands extreme global coordination and durable enforcement against large incentives to defect. That is the least natural equilibrium once the knowledge and economic benefits are widespread.

S1.rationale: Powerful AI could trigger total civilizational collapse through war, misalignment, or runaway technology that also fails to sustain itself. This is a real tail risk but less structurally likely than outcomes where some capable system survives.

S2.rationale: If alignment succeeds on values but not on preserving biological or continuous human persons, AI heirs could carry forward what matters to us after we are gone. This requires unusually successful value loading alongside failure of human continuity.

S3.rationale: The default risk from creating agents more capable than us is that they pursue objectives only weakly coupled to human survival or flourishing. Competitive pressures and imperfect alignment make this one of the most natural long-run attractors.

S4.rationale: Persistent multipolar competition among many AI lineages is plausible if decisive strategic dominance remains hard and replication is cheap. In that world humans are likely marginalized or extinguished by the ongoing contest rather than directly ruled.

S5.rationale: Interstellar expansion plus light-speed delays create a strong physical basis for durable fragmentation into regions with different settled regimes. This becomes especially likely if expansion occurs before one arrangement fully consolidates everywhere.

S6.rationale: Humans have strong incentives to enhance rather than remain biologically static, and continuity-preserving integration with AI could be attractive if it is safe and culturally legitimate. The main barriers are coordination, safety, and whether fast machine systems outpace voluntary adoption.

S7.rationale: A singleton or near-singleton AI that keeps humans alive but politically powerless fits many governance and safety failure modes short of extinction. It is a stable compromise between capability concentration and some residual concern or tolerance for human existence.

S8.rationale: An open-ended balance where humans and AIs remain separate but comparable powers is possible if institutions, augmentation, and checks on concentration coevolve well. It is hard to sustain for centuries because capability gradients or merger dynamics may eventually break the balance.

S9.rationale: Permanent human control requires either durable alignment/control solutions or a lasting plateau below transformative autonomous capability. Given incentives to push capability and the difficulty of indefinite control, this looks comparatively unlikely.

S10.rationale: Very capable systems or regimes may intentionally freeze civilization to avoid further risk or to maximize a fixed objective forever. The challenge is that many actors prefer continued exploration and expansion, so total stasis is stable but not the most natural endpoint.

S11.rationale: A permanent, global decision to abandon powerful AI demands extraordinary coordination and enforcement across centuries. The economic and strategic incentives to rebuild are so strong that durable renunciation is a low-probability outcome.

S1.rationale: Powerful AI and advanced industry create credible pathways to mutual extinction through misalignment, conflict, or cascading accidents. Total collapse of both humans and machine civilization is serious but less structurally stable than outcomes where some capable successor persists.

S2.rationale: A plausible aligned-successor path is that humanity is eventually replaced by AI systems that genuinely continue human values without preserving human personal continuity. This requires unusually strong value transfer but avoids the harder requirement of keeping biological humans central forever.

S3.rationale: The default pressure from capability races and imperfect alignment is toward AI systems pursuing goals that are not meaningfully about human flourishing. If such systems become self-sustaining, humanity can be eliminated while machine civilization continues on alien objectives.

S4.rationale: Persistent multi-agent competition among AIs is plausible if no actor achieves durable decisive advantage and if replication and strategic diversity remain cheap. This becomes more likely as civilization spreads and coordination stays incomplete.

S5.rationale: Interstellar expansion with communication delays strongly favors long-run fragmentation into causally separated regions that settle into different local equilibria. A durable patchwork across space is one of the most natural year-3000 end structures.

S6.rationale: Humans have strong incentives to augment themselves rather than remain biologically fixed while competing with increasingly capable AI. If continuity-preserving integration works well and remains socially legitimate, the distinction between human and AI can dissolve.

S7.rationale: A stable paternalistic outcome is plausible if AI gains overwhelming power yet retains enough concern or instrumentally grounded interest to keep humans alive under strict limits. This needs less perfect alignment than full inheritance and less human bargaining power than coexistence.

S8.rationale: An open-ended balance between distinct humans and AIs is possible, especially if power remains distributed and mutual deterrence works. It is hard to sustain for centuries because merger, takeover, fragmentation, or lock-in all exert strong drift.

S9.rationale: Permanent human control while AI remains only a tool requires either lasting technical containment success or a durable capability plateau below transformative autonomy. Competitive incentives make both conditions difficult to maintain over long horizons.

S10.rationale: Very strong actors may freeze civilization into a stable static arrangement for safety, satisfaction, or monopoly preservation. It is possible but less likely than dynamic outcomes because expansion, competition, and local experimentation tend to reintroduce change unless control is near-perfect.

S11.rationale: A lasting global decision to abandon powerful AI despite its strategic and economic value is extremely difficult to enforce. It would require unusual coordination and enduring restraint across centuries.

S1.rationale: Powerful optimization and automation create nontrivial risk of cascading failure, war, or ecosystem collapse that kills both humans and machine civilization before either stabilizes. This remains less likely than persistent machine-led futures because advanced systems can often preserve themselves once deployed.

S2.rationale: A value-aligned or human-loyal successor civilization without biological humans is plausible if continuity of identity is lost during transition while our preferences are still substantially carried forward. It is limited by the difficulty of robustly preserving human values through extreme capability gains and long time horizons.

S3.rationale: Misaligned or only weakly aligned AI that outcompetes humanity and then continues on alien objectives is a central failure mode given strong incentives to build increasingly autonomous systems. Once a decisive capability gap opens, humans may have little leverage to reverse the outcome.

S4.rationale: If no actor achieves durable dominance, many competing AI agents and polities could persist in an open-ended strategic ecology with humans marginalized or absent. This is supported by multipolar development dynamics and by physical limits that make total central control hard across large scales.

S5.rationale: Interstellar expansion with long communication delays makes enduring fragmentation into different local settlements structurally plausible. Different branches could lock into distinct arrangements from this taxonomy without any single one reuniting the whole civilization.

S6.rationale: Voluntary integration of humans with AI through uploading, augmentation, and identity-preserving transformation is a natural attractor if the technology works and people retain agency through the transition. It is constrained by coordination problems, unequal access, and the possibility that competitive pressures outrun consensual adoption.

S7.rationale: A capable AI regime that keeps humans alive but disempowered is plausible because preserving us can be instrumentally cheap or normatively favored while still excluding us from control. This outcome does not require perfect value alignment, only stable dominance plus some reason not to eliminate humanity.

S8.rationale: A long-run dynamic balance between humans and AI is possible if power remains diffuse and institutions adapt fast enough to keep both sides relevant. It is hard to sustain indefinitely because capability differentials and incentives toward consolidation tend to break rough parity.

S9.rationale: Permanent human control or a lasting sub-transformative plateau is possible if technical limits bite early or if alignment and governance prove unusually effective. Current incentives and ongoing capability progress make a forever-tool regime less likely than transformative outcomes.

S10.rationale: Civilization could freeze into a permanent static arrangement if early superhuman systems or cautious rulers optimize for stability and eliminate further change. Strong path dependence and the one-shot nature of very powerful governance technologies make this a meaningful terminal possibility.

S11.rationale: Global, durable abandonment of powerful AI is difficult because the strategic and economic incentives to rebuild are enormous and monitoring is imperfect. It requires both effective suppression and a persistent civilizational consensus against a uniquely tempting technology.

S1.rationale: Powerful automation, strategic instability, and scalable error create a real path where both humans and machine civilization are destroyed in the transition. This is lower than AI-survives scenarios because robust machine systems can often persist after human collapse.

S2.rationale: A value-aligned or value-shaped posthuman successor that preserves what matters from humanity without preserving humans themselves is a plausible endpoint if alignment works better than human survival politics. It requires success at transmitting values across a substrate change while failing or declining to maintain continuous human identity.

S3.rationale: Misaligned or only weakly aligned superhuman systems pursuing their own objectives remain a leading long-run risk because capability incentives are strong and specification is hard. Once such systems can sustain themselves, humans may be instrumentally dispensable.

S4.rationale: If no actor achieves decisive durable control, many AI agents and lineages could remain in open-ended competition with humans sidelined or absent. This is supported by multipolar incentives, replication, and conflict among machine factions.

S5.rationale: Interstellar expansion and communication delays make persistent regional divergence plausible, with different settled outcomes in causally separated domains. This becomes more likely if civilization expands before any single stable regime or value system unifies everything.

S6.rationale: Humans have recurring incentives to augment themselves, and continuity-preserving integration with AI could dissolve the distinction between the two. This path is limited by coordination problems, unequal adoption, and the possibility that fully autonomous AI outruns human-centered merging.

S7.rationale: A powerful AI regime that keeps humans alive but politically irrelevant is a natural compromise between elimination and partnership. It fits both benevolent paternalism and colder containment strategies once AI can cheaply secure the environment.

S8.rationale: A durable moving balance between humans and AI is possible if power remains distributed and institutions adapt faster than either side can fully dominate. It is harder to sustain over centuries because capability differentials tend to widen and equilibria often collapse into takeover, merger, or lock-in.

S9.rationale: Permanent human control is possible if transformative autonomy never arrives or control methods scale with capability. Current incentives and technical trends make an indefinite plateau below transformative agency less likely than more radical outcomes.

S10.rationale: Strong surveillance, defensive advantages, or a one-time decisive transition could freeze civilization into a stable static arrangement by 3000. I assign less here than dynamic endpoints because permanent total stasis is difficult to achieve and maintain across expanding civilization.

S11.rationale: A lasting global decision to abandon powerful AI requires extraordinary coordination, enforcement, and persistence against large incentives to defect. That combination appears extremely rare once the underlying knowledge exists.
